segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was the verb to give? Do you remember the verb to give?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Dar, good. So how would you say I will give?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And he will give, or she, you formal, it?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. How would you say will you guys give it to me? Now,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: me, me, can also mean to me, so we don't need that to.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And out of these little words, me, and what is the word for it?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Lo. So out of these little words, me and lo, the personal one, the one referring to the person, comes first.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Will you guys give it to me?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿Me lo darán? What if this it was a feminine thing?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿Me la darán? And I should clarify this isn't a way of requesting like in English, "will you guys give it to me" like "can you guys give it to me?" This is more of a literal question: are you guys going to give it to me, will you guys give it to me? If you want to get this meaning of "will you" like "can you", you will just use "can you" in Spanish. The word for something is algo, a-l-g-o.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So how would you say they will give you something, and we mean informal you?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Remember the thought process. The thought process must be first who is doing the verb. Who is doing the verb: they will give. That's the first place.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Te darán algo. Good. How would you say they will give it to you, still speaking informally, they will give it to you?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Te lo darán. They will give it to you. Good. How would you say they will give it to us? They will give it to us.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Nos lo darán. They will not give it to us.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No nos lo darán. So, we saw that me, te, nos can mean me or to me, you or to you, us or to us, or even in some other circumstances for me or for us, for you. Me, te, nos can also mean myself, yourself, and ourselves. For example, you can say I give myself, and you would just use me. So how would you say I give myself?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Me doy. If you want to say I realize in Spanish, you say me doy cuenta. Cuenta is something like account. To give yourself account of, to take account of, that's how you say I realize in Spanish. If you say realizar, it means to realize like a project, to bring into fruition. No? So you say I give myself account: cuenta. So how would you say that?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Me doy cuenta. This means I realize. You realize, talking informally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Te das cuenta. How would you make that a question?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿Te das cuenta? This is used a lot conversationally. ¿Te das cuenta? Do you realize? Do you know what I mean? Do you know what I'm saying? Good. We realize. We realize. We give ourselves account.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Nos damos cuenta. So, me can mean to me, for me, from me, it can mean myself. Te can mean you or to you, from you, yourself. And nos: us, to us, or ourselves, or each other. We said that you might hear nos vemos, we see each other, as a way to say ciao, goodbye, nos vemos, we see each other later, see you later. Now, you get all of these different meanings with me, te, and nos. But the ones beginning with L, so lo, la, los, las, they do change to get these different meanings.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, when we say to him, or to her, or to you formal, or to them, we go from lo and la and los and las to le and les. So lo and la becomes le, and los and las become les.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: For example, lo doy means I give it. Now if I want to say I give him, what I actually mean is I give to him. In which case here we must change to le. If I say I give her, I don't mean I'm going to pick her up and give her to somebody, I probably mean I give to her. In which case we're not going to use la, we're going to use le. So let's practice this a little bit.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we said dar is to give. Now if you say I give it, how do you say that?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Lo doy. And I give them, and you still are talking about the things you are giving?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Los doy. But now if you want to say I give them and you mean to them, so remember you might not even say this to in English, but what you mean is I give to them, then this los is going to change.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Les doy, good. The word for something was...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Algo. So let's say I'm giving them something.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Les doy algo. Good. So this is to them.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: To speak, to speak began with a silent h, I don't know if you remember this verb?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hablar. Good. So how do you say I speak?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hablo. How would you say I have spoken? I have...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes, he. So, I have spoken...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No, this is speaking, and spoken is very similar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: He hablado, good. I have spoken to him.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Le he hablado. I have spoken to him or to her, uh? Could be either. Now what if you wanted to say we have spoken to him?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Le hemos hablado. So this le, it could be the lo to le or the la to le. So many meanings are included here. It could be we have spoken to him, we have spoken to her, we have spoken to you formal, speaking to male or female. Le hemos hablado. How was he has or she has or it has from haber?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ha, good, h-a, ha. He has spoken?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Han hablado. They have spoken about it. They have spoken it.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. They have spoken to him or to her.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Le han hablado. They have spoken to them. I mean one them has spoken to a different them. They have spoken to them.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Les han hablado. Good. So we had ver, to see. The version for I see was a little bit irregular. How was it?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Veo, good. A little bit irregular. It's not vo, as it should be, v-o, it's veo, v-e-o, good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So if you want to say I see it, or I see him, or I see you, talking formally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Lo veo. What if you saw a feminine thing, or if you saw her, or if you saw you formal talking to a female?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: La veo. What if you were seeing las casas, what if you meant I see them, and you're referring to feminine things?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Las veo. And what else could it mean then, other than I see them talking about things?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yeah. I see them females, I see you guys females, or I see them feminine objects. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We said that the kitchen is la cocina. And to make the verb, you can just stick an r on cocina and you get...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Cocinar, with the accent on the end, cocinar. Now in English, if I say he's cooking me something, I can say he's cooking me something or he's cooking something for me. Both are acceptable in English. So we're not looking for the direct translation, we're looking for the feeling more than anything. We want to identify the feeling of is it to me, is it for me, or is it directly me. Is he cooking me? So it's the feeling that we want to get our heads around more than the direct translation of whether we're using to or not in English. For example, I listen to him. Here we're using to in English with listen, but we don't use it with hear: I hear him, I listen to him. So we're not looking for direct translation of when we're using to and for or not. What we're trying to do is generally perceive: okay, am I being cooked? Am I being spoken? Am I coming out of somebody's mouth, uh? Or is it indirect: am I being cooked for, am I being given to?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So like I said, with me, te, and nos it doesn't matter anyway because they won't change. So if I want to say he's cooking me and I mean he's directly cooking me in the oven, or if I mean he's cooking something for me, then the sentence isn't going to change anyway in Spanish. So how would you say that: he is cooking me something, he's cooking me something?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Me cocina algo. Now let's say he's cooking something for us.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Nos cocina algo. He's cooking something for you, speaking informally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So me, te, nos we don't have to worry about them, they don't, they don't change. But if I want to say he is cooking him something, how would I say it?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. How would you say he is cooking them something?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Les cocina algo. What if you wanted to say he is cooking them, and with this them you are referring to the things he is cooking, not to the people he is cooking for?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We don't need the algo anymore.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Los cocina. And if he was cooking feminine things, like las tartas, the tarts for example, how would it be: he's cooking them?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Now if you wanted to say he's cooking them for us, and we still mean feminine things, let's stay with las tartas, he's cooking them for us, how would it be?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Perfect. We don't need for or any of this, and we put the personal one first: nos las cocina, good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Le hablo. Good. And I'm speaking to them?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. They are speaking to them?
